segment:
He wasn’t breathing hard. His hands hung loosely at his sides, and she couldn’t see what they were doing. She kept her hands still.
They passed the darkened reception hall without stopping to wait for the night desk clerk. The front door swung shut behind them, but he didn’t stop and turn back. She felt the lock click in the wood.
Outside, the breeze was cool, almost cold. But the wind smelled like the sea, a strong sweet-briny tang that reminded her of nothing so much as the way Jonah smelled: salt and ozone and something deeper, the animal warmth he didn’t always mask with cologne. She’d noticed it almost the first time she’d seen him, in the first session she’d attended at Fulcrum three weeks before.
It hadn’t mattered then; the scent had been nothing more than an observation. But it mattered now. She smelled him from his back.
There were no street lamps between Fulcrum and the downtown area. She could have seen where she was going, but Jonah didn’t look to check whether or not she was there; he went straight on as if she were a ghost following behind him.
He didn’t speak for almost a block before turning into the first lane of a side street. Mara stopped at the corner, one hand touching a lamp post. It was cold metal under her palm. Jonah hesitated. She thought she saw him turn to look back at her, though he didn’t speak, but when he realized she wasn’t coming, he moved on again.
He walked quickly, even more rapidly than before. She felt the pull of him going faster ahead of her, as if he were moving forward in a stream and leaving her behind on the bank.
Mara tried to breathe at the same rate he had, but it didn’t help. Her lungs ached, and her head began to clear; she could feel the first tremors of exhaustion under the adrenaline.
Her knees felt weak. She stood still. She wanted him to come back.
The walk took longer than it should have. She had been there a few times since the first day, and she knew that it didn’t take a quarter of an hour to reach the hotel from Fulcrum.
It wasn’t so far. She was just tired.
But he would probably turn the corner at the end of this street; if she didn’t move soon, she’d lose him in the next block.
Mara started walking again. It felt like a dream when her feet moved and she saw the sidewalk move beneath them, as though she were in one of the lab chairs, watching another subject move in real time. She had no sensation of moving her legs or taking steps; it was only when she saw her feet on the sidewalk that she knew she was actually walking.
text:
They started at Fulcrum’s front steps, an instant after the last of the lab staff had gone indoors and locked up. Mara’s mouth felt raw and dry; her throat ached, and her shoulders were rigid and aching too. Her entire body was too hot despite the cold, and she didn’t feel the chill of the night air.
The others were gone. Jonah stood silently beside her, waiting. He was six inches taller than she was. He wasn’t looking at her; his head turned toward the empty drive, and he stared into the darkness beyond the lighted entrance. There was nothing there. She didn’t look. She watched him instead.
“I guess it’s time to go home.” Jonah’s voice was soft, almost inaudible. She had expected more after tonight: analysis or commiseration. Instead he turned sideways with a small sigh and started down the front steps. He swung both arms easily, as though he were on an ordinary walk, though it was the middle of the night and they were both on their way back to hotel rooms in a town she didn’t know.
She followed, trying to match his step. His dark hair rustled as he moved, a low whisper that went with the sound of his breathing: slow, even, no sign of anxiety.

segment:
The muscles of his shoulders relaxed and curved around his neck. They’d just gone through the most invasive, most embarrassing day she could remember, and he seemed unaffected by it.
She wished he’d been one of the others in the room tonight instead of her. She didn’t want to share her humiliation with him. He’d just seen something she couldn’t have shown anyone else. Jonah knew nothing about her childhood, but the experiment tonight had changed that. Her carefully guarded privacy had been exposed to strangers who were also her professional peers. Jonah’s eyes might be empty and averted, but his face hadn’t changed tonight, and she didn’t know what he was feeling.
He stopped at the bottom of the steps and turned to her without looking at her face. “You okay?” It was a question but his tone made it sound like a command. He waited without moving while she checked her body for an answer. She looked him in the face. She hoped he’d tell her what he was thinking, but when she said nothing he took a step toward her as though she were answering. His mouth moved to speak but no sound came out. He nodded at the road that led back into town. “This way?”
She thought about going home alone: the relief of solitude, the warm bath in her hotel room, and bed without his presence or his touch. She took a deep breath and opened her mouth to answer. He reached into the sleeve pocket of his jacket. When he pulled his hand back out he held a cell phone. “Do you have your car?” It wasn’t a question. His voice was low, neutral. “Let me know when we get there. I can follow.”
She waited to see if he’d ask something else or do something more. Her breath came quickly now. She wanted him to be honest. She didn’t know what she could trust. His shoulders dropped without moving, as though he were getting used to the weight of his jacket. The gesture was unconscious and slow but it made her relax her throat.
